newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Kangaroos bonds could make first leap in 1997.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Kangaroos bonds could make first leap in 1997.

text.p: Australia's kangaroo bonds could make an increased impact on the country's debt investment profile next year as more foreign borrowers enter the market and local investors diversify their portfolios.
The kangaroo market is still in its infancy with three transactions from Korean borrowers having been launched.

But "as the growth in funds under management begins to come through in the second half of 1997, the capacity for new borrowers to come from other markets grows quite strongly", said Wayne Hoy, Chief Manager Financial Markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Kangaroo bonds are issued by foreign borrowers in the Australian domestic market.

Shrinking investment assets as the Federal government and state governments rein back their debt issuance programmes means that growing funds from compulsory superannuation savings will see a need for a diversification.

"There is a growing gap between the supply and demand of securities in Australia. We estimate there to be in the order of A$50 billion per annum by the year 2000," Ian Moore, executive Vice President at Bankers Trust Australia, told RFTV.
"With a gap of that size investors are going to have to diversify their credit exposures offshore and Asia," Moore said.
However, he felt supply in the kangaroo market will remain only open to investment grade credits at this stage, and traditionally the limit of local superannuation funds investments.
While CBA and BT Australia are confident about the growth of kangaroos, there has been some criticsim over the lack of liquidity and tight pricing of the instruments.

"I think the threat is that we will try to over-reach in terms of pricing, but each of these transactions is being price talked with investors before the structures are brought to the market, so that minimises the basis for error," CBA's Hoy said.
And while he agreed that there has not been much secondary play in the issues, Hoy saw this as a sign that investors were happy to keep hold of these assets.
